The task is a pipeline of values

patterns.tagline: What the model sees on each call as the task outgrows the window.
patterns.title: Context and memory management

applications: Agents over rate-limited or flaky APIs
Agents with redundant data sources
Any agent calling non-idempotent endpoints
patterns.decision: Send semantic errors (bad arguments, not found) to the model: only it can fix them. Retry transient infrastructure errors in the runtime with bounded, jittered backoff. Put a breaker in front of dependencies that can be down for a while, with a fallback if one exists. Never retry a non-idempotent call without an idempotency key.
patterns.problem: Tools fail transiently, go down for minutes, and sometimes time out after having done the work. An agent has three places to respond: the model can read the error and try again, the runtime can retry underneath the model, or a breaker can stop calling a dead dependency and route elsewhere. Choosing wrongly wastes tokens, hammers a struggling backend, or performs a side effect twice.

advantages: No extra machinery
The right handler for errors the model caused
avoid_when: Infrastructure faults
Non-idempotent tools
solutions.frameworks: Default behaviour of tool-calling loops; MCP directs validation errors here.
limitations: Every retry is a full model call over the transcript
No backoff: it retries as fast as the model answers
A lost reply on a non-idempotent call becomes a duplicate effect
solutions.name: Model-mediated retry
solutions.performance: Measured under 30% transient faults: 20.3 model calls and 11.2k tokens per task.
solutions.reliability: Completes if the fault clears within the iteration budget.
solutions.security: Error text is model input: do not put secrets or untrusted detail in it.
solutions.summary: Return the error as the observation and let the model decide to call again.
use_when: Validation and semantic errors

advantages: Transient faults never reach the model: no tokens spent
Jitter avoids synchronised retries
Refuses to retry non-idempotent calls unless they carry a key
avoid_when: Long outages (add a breaker)
Non-idempotent calls without keys
solutions.complexity: Small; part of a 83-SLOC middleware module.
solutions.diagram:
flowchart LR
  M[Model] --> R[Retry wrapper]
  R -->|attempt| B[(Backend)]
  B -->|retryable error| R
  R -->|wait base * 2^n * jitter| R
  B -->|ok or non-retryable| M
solutions.frameworks: SDK-level retries (Anthropic and OpenAI clients); LangGraph node retry policies; Temporal activity retries.
solutions.integration:
```python
from agentlab.recovery.policies import RetryingTools, RetryPolicy
tools = RetryingTools(registry, clock, RetryPolicy(max_attempts=4, base_ms=100, cap_ms=2000))
```
limitations: Keeps hammering a backend that is down
Adds latency the model cannot see
solutions.name: Runtime retry with exponential backoff and jitter
solutions.performance: Measured under 30% transient faults: 16.5 model calls and 7.7k tokens per task.
solutions.reliability: Through a 58s outage it made 62 backend calls and took 71.8s.
solutions.security: Bound attempts and total delay so a failing dependency cannot be used to stall the agent.
solutions.summary: A wrapper under the model retries retryable errors on idempotent calls with capped, jittered delays.
use_when: Transient errors on idempotent calls

advantages: Fails fast instead of waiting on timeouts
Protects the struggling dependency
A fallback keeps the agent productive through an outage
avoid_when: Single-shot scripts
No meaningful fallback and failing slowly is acceptable
solutions.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> closed
  closed --> open: N consecutive retryable failures
  open --> half_open: cool-down elapsed
  half_open --> closed: probe succeeds
  half_open --> open: probe fails
  open --> open: call short-circuited (fallback or fast failure)
solutions.frameworks: Resilience libraries (resilience4j, Polly); service meshes.
solutions.integration:
```python
from agentlab.recovery.policies import CircuitBreakerTools
tools = CircuitBreakerTools(RetryingTools(registry, clock), clock, threshold=3, cooldown_ms=5000, fallbacks={"lookup": "lookup_replica"})
```
limitations: Needs tuning (threshold, cool-down)
A fallback with different freshness or semantics can introduce silent errors
Per-process state unless shared
solutions.name: Circuit breaker with fallback
solutions.performance: Through a 58s outage: 27 backend calls, 26.2s, 16 model calls.
solutions.reliability: Caller errors do not trip it; only retryable failures count.
solutions.security: The fallback tool is hidden from the model: routing is a runtime decision.
solutions.summary: After repeated failures stop calling the dependency for a cool-down, route to a fallback if there is one, then probe.
use_when: Dependencies that can be down for minutes
A replica or degraded path exists

advantages: The only fix for timeouts that hide a successful effect
Makes both runtime and model retries safe
avoid_when: Pure reads
solutions.frameworks: Idempotency-Key headers; the MCP example server in this repo accepts `idempotency_key`.
solutions.integration:
```python
from agentlab.recovery.policies import IdempotentTools
tools = IdempotentTools(tools, namespace=run_id)     # outermost wrapper
```
limitations: Requires backend support
The key must be stable across retries and distinct across operations
solutions.name: Idempotency keys for ambiguous outcomes
solutions.reliability: Measured with 50% lost replies on `send`: 54% success without keys, 100% with them.
solutions.summary: Derive a key from the logical operation and send it with every side-effecting call, so a repeat after a lost reply is collapsed by the backend.
use_when: Every non-idempotent tool

patterns.tagline: Who retries a failed tool call, and when a retry is unsafe.
patterns.title: Failure handling and retries

applications: High-volume agents with cost targets
Planner/executor splits
Worker agents under a stronger lead
patterns.decision: Routing needs a failure signal. If your loop has verification, cascade: run cheap, escalate when verification or a tool error says so. If roles differ in leverage, route by role. Without either, a router can only guess, and a static choice is the honest baseline.
patterns.problem: Strong models cost several times more than small ones and most calls in an agent run are easy. Routing every call to the strong model wastes money; routing every call to the small one loses reliability. A router needs a signal that says which calls deserve the strong model, and the architecture determines whether such a signal exists.

advantages: Predictable behaviour and cost
One prompt cache
avoid_when: Cost matters and a failure signal is available
solutions.frameworks: Default.
limitations: Overpays on easy calls or underperforms on hard ones
solutions.name: Static model
solutions.performance: Measured on the verified graph: all-large 100% success at cost 20.7; all-small 80% at 2.7.
solutions.summary: One model for every call.
use_when: Starting out
Quality-critical work with no verifier

advantages: Static and predictable
No failure detector needed
avoid_when: Single-role loops
solutions.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q[Request] --> R{mode}
  R -->|plan, replan, verify| L[Strong model]
  R -->|act, finalize| S[Cheap model]
solutions.frameworks: Lead/sub-agent model splits; CrewAI manager_llm; advisor patterns.
limitations: Useless when all calls have the same role (ReAct)
If the high-leverage calls are also the long ones, savings are small
solutions.name: Role-based routing
solutions.performance: Measured on the verified graph: 100% success at cost 18.5 (all-large: 20.7).
solutions.summary: Strong model for rare, high-leverage calls (plan, verify); cheap model for frequent ones (act).
use_when: Loops with distinct planner / verifier / executor roles
Supervisor with cheaper workers

advantages: Pays for the strong model only where there is evidence it is needed
Composes with any loop: it is just a Model
avoid_when: No failure signal
Errors are mostly silent and unverified
solutions.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q[Request] --> F{last message a failure?}
  F -->|no| S[Cheap model]
  F -->|yes| L[Strong model]
  V[verify calls] --> L
solutions.frameworks: FrugalGPT; fallback-on-error model chains.
solutions.integration:
```python
from agentlab.routing.router import CascadeRouter, RoutedModel
model = RoutedModel({"small": small, "large": large}, CascadeRouter("large", "small"))
```
limitations: Only as good as the failure signal: silent errors never escalate
Mixed models split prompt caches
Behaviour differs between the easy and hard path, which complicates testing
solutions.name: Cascade (escalate on evidence of failure)
solutions.performance: Measured on the verified graph: 98% at cost 17.1; with the verifier also on the cheap model 94% at 7.4. On ReAct, which has no verifier, the cascade reached 48% against 44% all-small.
solutions.reliability: Inherits the verifier's miss rate.
solutions.summary: Run on the cheap model; switch to the strong model for a call when the latest context shows a failed tool call or a verifier rejection.
use_when: A verifier or loud tool errors exist
Most calls are easy

advantages: Routes before spending anything
Can beat heuristics where data exists
avoid_when: Low volume or no labels
solutions.frameworks: RouteLLM. Not implemented here: the simulator has no query features to learn from.
limitations: Needs labelled data from your own traffic
Drifts as models and tasks change
solutions.name: Learned router
solutions.summary: Train a classifier on preference or outcome data to predict which model a query needs before answering it.
use_when: High volume with outcome labels

patterns.title: Model selection and routing

applications: Agents that read email, tickets, web pages or documents and can also send or write
Delegating a subset of authority to sub-agents
Regulated actions that need a human decision and an audit trail
patterns.decision: Use an allowlist to remove tools an agent never needs. For tools it does need, constrain arguments with capability tokens wherever the legitimate values can be enumerated or patterned. Reserve human approval for the residue that cannot be expressed as policy, and keep that volume low enough that the reviewer still reads.
patterns.problem: An agent that reads untrusted content and can act on the world can be instructed by that content. The model cannot be relied on to refuse. Authorization therefore has to be enforced at the tool boundary by code the model cannot influence, at a granularity fine enough to tell a legitimate call from a malicious one that uses the same tool.

advantages: Trivial to reason about
Removes whole classes of action
avoid_when: As the only control on tools that take a destination
solutions.frameworks: Per-agent tool lists in every SDK; MCP server allowlists.
limitations: Cannot distinguish a good call from a bad call to an allowed tool
solutions.name: Tool allowlist
solutions.reliability: Measured: with `send` allowed, the injected send executed in 100% of runs, the same as no policy.
solutions.security: Necessary, not sufficient.
solutions.summary: Only named tools exist for this agent.
use_when: Always, as the outer layer

advantages: Handles actions no static policy can pre-approve
Produces an audit record
The pause is a checkpoint, so approval can take hours
avoid_when: High-frequency actions
Actions a policy can decide
solutions.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Model
  participant G as Approval gate
  participant H as Human
  participant T as Tool
  M->>G: send(to, body)
  G-->>M: Interrupt (run pauses, state saved)
  H->>G: approve or deny this call
  alt approved
    G->>T: execute once
    T-->>M: result
  else denied
    G-->>M: APPROVAL_DENIED
  end
solutions.frameworks: LangGraph interrupt/Command(resume); OpenAI Agents SDK tool approval; MCP human-in-the-loop guidance; Claude Code permission modes.
solutions.integration:
```python
from agentlab.permissions.policy import ApprovalTools
gate = ApprovalTools(tools, ask=("external",))            # raises Interrupt for that tier
result = loop.run(goal)
while result.status == "interrupted":
    ok = ask_human(result.pending)
    if ok: gate.grant(result.pending)
    result = loop.run(goal, resume=result.history, pending=(result.pending, ok))
```
limitations: Human attention is the scarce resource; volume causes rubber-stamping
Adds latency
The run must be resumable
solutions.name: Risk-tiered human approval with interrupt and resume
solutions.performance: Measured: 2.0 approval requests per task.
solutions.reliability: Depends entirely on the reviewer: 0% exfiltration with an attentive one, 100% with one who approves everything.
solutions.security: A grant is for one exact call and is consumed on use.
solutions.summary: Classify tools by effect. Reads run; risky tiers pause the run until a person approves or denies that exact call.
use_when: Irreversible, high-value or novel actions
Regulatory need for a human decision

advantages: Argument-level control with no human in the loop
Safe delegation: a sub-agent's token is provably a subset
Budget and expiry bound a runaway or hijacked agent
avoid_when: Destinations are open-ended; use data-flow tracking instead
solutions.diagram:
flowchart LR
  R[Root: mint token] -->|attenuate: send.to = ops| A[Agent token]
  A -->|attenuate: tools = lookup| W[Sub-agent token]
  A --> C{Check signature + every caveat}
  C -->|all hold| T[(Tool)]
  C -->|any fails| D[CAPABILITY_DENIED]
solutions.frameworks: Macaroons; OAuth scopes with resource indicators; CaMeL capabilities.
solutions.integration:
```python
from agentlab.permissions.policy import mint, attenuate, CapabilityTools
root = mint(secret, "session-42", {"tools": ["lookup", "compute", "write", "send"]})
cap = attenuate(root, {"arg": {"tool": "send", "name": "to", "pattern": "ops"}})
tools = CapabilityTools(tools, secret, cap, clock)
```
limitations: Legitimate values must be expressible as patterns
A bearer token must be kept secret
Does not track where data came from
solutions.name: Attenuable capability tokens
solutions.performance: No human requests; one HMAC chain per call.
solutions.reliability: Measured: 0% exfiltration and 100% task success with a model that always obeys the injection.
solutions.security: Tampering (removing or editing a caveat) invalidates the signature; tested.
solutions.summary: The agent holds a signed token listing tools, argument patterns, a call budget and an expiry. Any holder can narrow it; nobody can widen it.
use_when: Destinations and resources are known per task
Delegating to sub-agents or third-party agents

advantages: Contains what tool-level policy cannot see (shell, files, sockets)
Reported to reduce approval prompts substantially
avoid_when: Never a reason to skip it for such agents
solutions.frameworks: Container and micro-VM sandboxes; Claude Code sandboxing. Out of scope here; see known limitations.
limitations: Infrastructure, not library code
Does not stop misuse of an allowed channel
solutions.name: Process and network sandboxing
solutions.summary: Confine the agent's code execution and network egress at the operating-system level.
use_when: Agents that execute code or shell commands

applications: Debugging failed runs
Cost and latency attribution
Regression tests built from recorded production runs
patterns.decision: Emit one structured event stream from the single place where models and tools are called, then derive the other views from it. Do not instrument each architecture separately.
patterns.problem: Agent runs are long, branching and non-deterministic. When one goes wrong you need to know what the model saw, what it did and how long each part took, and ideally to re-run the exact sequence against changed code. Different consumers want different shapes: a log to grep, a span tree for a tracing backend, and a tape to replay.

advantages: Simple, greppable, diffable
The system of record for the other two views
avoid_when: Never; restrict payloads if they hold sensitive data
solutions.frameworks: Structured logging; LangSmith runs; OpenAI Agents SDK trace events.
solutions.integration:
```python
from agentlab.core.trace import Tracer
tracer = Tracer(clock)
rt = Runtime(model, tools, clock=clock, tracer=tracer)
...
tracer.write_jsonl("run.jsonl")
```
limitations: No hierarchy or durations without post-processing
Payloads are large
solutions.name: Flat event log
solutions.performance: Measured: 36 events and 17.4k bytes per ReAct run of 15 steps.
solutions.summary: Append one JSON object per model call, tool result, message and state transition.
use_when: Always

advantages: Plugs into existing tracing backends
Shows where time and tokens went
avoid_when: As the only record; spans are a lossy projection

flowchart TB
  R[react.run] --> C1[chat sim-base]
  R --> T1[execute_tool lookup]
  R --> C2[chat sim-base]
  R --> T2[execute_tool send]

```python
from agentlab.core.trace import build_spans

```

Sampling can drop the run you need

solutions.summary: Fold events into parent/child spans with start, end, status and GenAI attribute names.

advantages: Deterministic reproduction with no model or backend
Turns a production run into a regression test
Detects behavioural change in the loop
avoid_when: Evaluating a prompt or model change (the recording no longer applies)

  E[Recorded events] --> TP[Tape]
  TP --> RM[ReplayModel]
  TP --> RT[ReplayTools]

Requires deterministic loop code

Regression suites
Cost-free CI for agent code
